title: Coffee mug
hook: A mug holds 350 ml of coffee at 85 °C, and you can carry it across a room without burning your hand or spilling a drop. It looks like it has no mechanism at all.
It has two parts: a thick ceramic cup and a loop on its side. Why that loop, why that much ceramic, and why it's shaped the way it is all follow from a few small failures.

chapters.need: It must hold a hot drink.
chapters.why: This is the object's job: keep 350 ml of near-boiling liquid in one place long enough to drink it.

steps.title: An open-topped cylinder
story: The simplest container is a cylinder closed at the bottom and open at the top. Make it 80 mm across and 95 mm tall and it holds about 400 ml, enough for 350 ml of coffee with room so it doesn't slop over the rim.

Ceramic is fired clay. It doesn't rust, doesn't flavour the drink and doesn't soften at 100 °C. Its glaze is a layer of glass fused onto the surface, and it closes the clay's pores so the liquid can't soak in. No moving part is needed for that, so no primitive here.

problem.outcome: It holds all 350 ml without leaking. With a 1.5 mm wall, though, the outside reaches about 80 °C within ten seconds, only 5 °C below the coffee itself.

payoff: The cup body does its first job: it holds the liquid. But a thin wall passes heat almost straight through, so the outside is nearly as hot as the drink.

steps.title: Thicken the wall
story: Heat crosses a wall at a rate that falls as the wall gets thicker, and ceramic conducts heat poorly to begin with, about a thousandth as well as copper. A thicker wall also holds more heat itself, so once it has warmed up it gives that heat back to the coffee rather than taking more from it.

problem.outcome: The outside now settles around 60–65 °C instead of 80 °C, and the empty cup's mass rises from about 120 g to 350 g. Skin still burns on 60 °C ceramic after a few seconds of contact.

payoff: That's why mug walls are thick: the wall slows heat on its way out and acts as a heat store. It isn't enough to make the outside safe to hold, and the extra mass will come back later in the lesson. This model ignores heat lost through the open top, which is actually the largest loss.

chapters.need: It must be lifted without burning the hand.
chapters.why: The wall still sits at about 60 °C, and the only way to lift the cup so far is to hold that wall.

steps.title: Squeeze the hot wall
story: Holding a smooth cylinder from the sides relies on friction. Fingers and thumb press inward, and the cup can't slide down until its weight beats μ times the total squeeze. For skin on glaze, μ is about 0.4.
A full mug weighs about 6.5 N. A jolt, a tilt or a damp glaze can easily triple that demand, so treat the load as 20 N.

problem.goal: With the load at 20 N, set the squeeze so the friction limit is at least 20 N while each finger presses as little as possible on the 60 °C wall.
problem.tooLow: Below 25 N per pad the limit is under 20 N (μ × 2 × 24 = 19 N), and the mug slides out of your hand on the first jolt.
problem.tooHigh: Above 35 N per pad the fingertips flatten against the 60 °C glaze. More skin touches the hot wall, and it hurts within a second or two.
problem.justRight: Between 25 and 35 N per pad, the limit of 20–28 N covers the load with no wasted pressure.

payoff: The grip holds, but only for about two seconds. Friction needs pressure, and pressure pushes skin onto the hot wall. Any hold that touches the wall will fail for the same reason.

steps.title: Hold it somewhere cooler
story: We need to carry the cup's weight with fingers that never touch the wall. That means something attached to the cup that sticks out into cooler air, which the fingers can take hold of without squeezing.

problem.question: What can carry the cup's weight while the fingers stay away from the hot wall?

options.outcome: A rigid arm molded onto the wall reaches about 25 mm out. Fingers hook under it, so the shape carries the load instead of friction. The arm passes the cup's weight and its twisting effect back to the hand.
Squeezing harder only raises the friction limit. The fingers are still on the 60 °C wall, and pressing harder puts more skin against it.
A loop of string would hang the cup without touching the wall, but string can't push. The cup swings freely below your hand and tips coffee out as soon as you move.

payoff: This is the handle: a rigid lever molded onto the body. The fingers hook through it, so the hold depends on the handle's shape rather than on squeeze, and no squeeze means very little heat reaches the skin.
Ceramic carries heat slowly, so a handle 25 mm long cools along its length. Where the fingers sit it's about 40 °C, warm but safe to hold.

steps.title: The weight is off-centre
story: The fingers are now off to one side, but the cup's weight acts at its centre. That makes a lever: the hook point is the pivot, and the weight pulls down about 65 mm away from it.

problem.outcome: The mug tries to rotate away from the hand with a torque of 6.5 N × 0.065 m ≈ 0.42 N·m. The thumb on top of the handle and the fingers below hold against it from about 20 mm apart, which takes about 21 N. The wrist manages it easily, and the cup stays level.

payoff: This is why a handle is a loop and not a peg. The top of the loop gives the thumb something to press on and the bottom gives the fingers something to hook under, so together they resist the twist.

chapters.need: It must stay upright on the table.
chapters.why: With a handle sticking out on one side, a nudge from a hand reaching for it is enough to rock the cup.

steps.title: Nudge a light cup
story: Imagine we'd kept the 1.5 mm wall to save material. An empty 120 g cup with a handle sits on the table, and a hand reaching for the handle brushes it from the side.

problem.outcome: A sideways push of about 0.6 N at the handle's height is enough to tip the light cup over its 70 mm foot. Half-full, it slides about 15 mm and the coffee slops over the rim.

payoff: A light cup is easy to tip and easy to slide. Whatever resists a careless hand has to be something the cup already has.

steps.title: What resists the nudge
story: To tip over, a cup has to lift its own centre over the edge of its foot. Sliding it means overcoming friction, which depends on how hard the cup presses down. Both resistances grow with one thing.

problem.question: What makes the cup shrug off a 0.6 N brush?

options.outcome: The 350 g ceramic body weighs 3.4 N and resists being moved. Tipping it now takes about 2 N at the handle, and its inertia soaks up a quick brush before it can move much.
A rubber pad on the foot raises μ and stops sliding. But tipping lifts the cup off the pad, so the pad does nothing against it.
A sprung base would push back on a nudge, but it gives the energy straight back too. The cup rocks and the coffee sloshes harder.

payoff: The thick wall we chose to block heat also gives the cup its weight. One choice of 5 mm of ceramic both keeps the outside cooler and keeps the cup steady.

steps.title: Across the room
story: Now everything works together: 350 ml at 85 °C, a 5 mm ceramic wall, a molded loop handle, and a total mass of about 700 g.

problem.outcome: The fingers stay about 25 mm from the wall and touch glaze at around 40 °C. The 0.42 N·m twist is held without effort. Set down, the cup needs about 3 N at the handle to tip, and the coffee stays above 60 °C for about 20 minutes.

payoff: Each requirement is met, and the parts overlap: the wall that slows heat also adds the weight, and the handle that keeps fingers off the wall also resists the twist.

steps.title: Why it looks like this
story: The body is a cylinder rather than a bowl. A tall, narrow shape exposes less coffee surface to the air, and its upright wall gives the handle something to attach to.

The handle's opening is about 25 by 50 mm, big enough for two or three fingers, and it's molded in the same firing as the body. A glued joint would creep under repeated heat. A fused joint is a single piece of ceramic that carries the twist.

problem.outcome: After 1000 cycles through hot water there are no seams to leak and no joint to loosen. The only failure left is the one ceramic always has: a 1 m drop onto tile breaks it.

payoff: Every feature you can see has a reason. The thickness is for heat and stability, the cylinder is for less surface and a wall to hold the handle, the loop is for the twist, and molding it in one piece makes the joint last.

closing: The mug you pick up now explains itself. Its wall is thick to slow heat and to add weight, the loop keeps your fingers off the hot ceramic and resists the twist, and the whole thing is fired as one piece. It has no moving parts, but every bit of it is there for a reason.
